<description>
{
 "summary": "Prevents the built-in HTTP server from reading or executing requests pipelined behind a \"Connection: close\" request. The server now tracks when a closing reply has been queued or a disconnection has been flagged, aborting further request parsing on that connection even if additional bytes remain in the receive buffer.",
 "problem": "After the replacement of libevent in #35182, the HTTP server continued to parse and dispatch pipelined requests sitting in the receive buffer after queuing a close response. Once the close response was sent, the server disconnected the client and dropped subsequent replies; per RFC 9112 \u00a79.6, clients expecting unserved requests to be unexecuted may retry them, leading to duplicate execution of RPCs with side effects.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'RFC 9112 section 9.6 requires a server that sends a close response not to process any further requests on that connection. A client that relies on this and resends the request executes it twice, which matters for RPCs with side effects.'",
  "PR description: 'The libevent based server freed the connection right after writing the close reply (evhttp_send_done() \u2192 evhttp_connection_free()), discarding any pipelined bytes, so this is a regression from #35182.'"
 ],

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
